entries.summary: Shift Briefing says when the delivery lands, not just that there is one
entries.details:
- The Shift Briefing's delivery flag now shows the time delivery lands.
- It also says whether you're still on when it does, or whether it lands before
  you start / after you finish.

Details:

Now that delivery schedules carry a target time (v5.7.0), the briefing card was
the last place still reducing it to a yes/no "Delivery day" badge — which on an
evening delivery tells you least on exactly the shifts where it matters most.

The badge now reads "Delivery 18:00 — you're on" when your shift covers the
delivery, using the same target ± 1 hour window Insights counts by, so the two
pages can't disagree about whether a shift was a delivery shift. When it doesn't
cover it, the badge drops to informational and says which side you miss it on
("Delivery day — 18:00, after you finish") rather than warning you about a
delivery you'll never see.

/api/v3/briefing gains a `delivery` object (is_delivery_day, time, on_shift).
The flat `delivery_day` boolean stays in the response for anything still reading
it, and the client falls back to it when the new object is absent.

entries.summary: Delivery schedules carry a target time, and Insights counts the shifts that covered it
entries.details:
- Delivery schedules now have a Delivery time as well as delivery days, set in
  Settings alongside the days.
- The dashboard's delivery weather is taken at that time instead of a hardcoded
  06:00, so both the time shown and the temperature next to it are right.
- Insights counts a delivery shift as one that was on the floor across the
  delivery window (the target time ± 1 hour), not one that merely started early.
- Times are kept as history the same way days already were, so past shifts stay
  judged against the delivery time that was actually in force back then.

Details:

The delivery hour was never configurable — delivery_schedules stored only
effective_from and days, and the hour lived in commute.js as `const
DELIVERY_HOUR = 6` with a comment explaining that delivery lands before the
store opens. That assumption is wrong now, and it was wrong in two places at
once: the "Delivery (06:00)" label on the next-shift card and the forecast hour
that label's temperature was read from.

delivery_schedules gains a delivery_time column, defaulting to 18:00 and
backfilled to 18:00 for existing rows — those rows were written when the hour
was hardcoded, so they carry no time of their own and there's no record of it
ever having been anything else. Editing a schedule sets the time for that
period only; adding a new row with a later effective_from is still how a change
is recorded, so the history keeps working exactly as it did for days.

The Insights "Delivery shifts" stat had the same assumption baked in from the
other end: it matched `start_time >= '05:30' AND start_time <= '08:00'` on a
delivery day, i.e. "you opened up". Against an 18:00 delivery that matches
nothing at all — a 14:00–18:45 shift covers the delivery but starts four hours
before the window. The rule is now overlap against the window: started before it
shut, finished after it opened. That reads the same for a morning delivery (an
06:45 start still overlaps 05:00–07:00), so old periods keep counting what they
always counted.

Because each delivery_schedules row now contributes its own branch to the SQL
CASE with its own window, a shift from a period when delivery landed at 06:00 is
still tested against 05:00–07:00 even though today's schedule says 18:00. That's
the whole reason the time is a column on the history table rather than a single
setting.

The window maths, the HH:MM validation and the CASE builder moved into
delivery.js so the weather overlay and the Insights query share one definition
instead of three copies of 18:00, and so they can be tested — test/
delivery-window.test.js covers the window bounds and clamping, the form
validation, the overlap rule, and the per-period history behaviour. It asserts
on the generated SQL rather than executing it: better-sqlite3 is a native build,
so like the other tests here it stays dependency-free.

entries.summary: Employee selection on Record Book and Rota Bingo
entries.details:
- Record Book and Rota Bingo now have an Employee picker like Insights/Shift
  DNA/Head to Head, showing a reduced but genuinely real view for a colleague.
- Audited the other pages on the original shortlist (Trophies, Balance, Year
  in Numbers, Crystal Ball, Did You Know) and left them alone — explained why
  below.

Details:

colleague_shifts only ever stores date/start/end — no break, pay, distance,
bank-holiday flag, contract or clock-in — so a colleague view can only ever
be as honest as that. Record Book now computes a colleague's shift-shape
records (longest/shortest shift, earliest start, latest finish, most/least
worked day, signature start time) straight from colleague_shifts rather than
reusing careerStats(), and simply omits the groups that need data colleagues
don't have (Clock in & out, pay/payslip records) instead of faking them.
Bingo works the same way at square level: every square whose test needs
pay/clock/contract/leave data (over_contract, ton_up, no_breaks, skipped,
punctual, bank_hol, no_drive, note_left, leave_day, big_week — 10 of 27) is
flagged colleague_blind and shown struck through and dimmed rather than
hidden, so it's visible that a colleague's card genuinely can't win those
squares rather than looking like an unlucky week. The other ~18 squares,
built purely from shift shape, tick normally.

Trophies, Balance, Year in Numbers and Crystal Ball were left out after
checking their actual data dependencies (not just their names): Trophies'
persisted unlock tiers (v3_trophy_unlocks) have no colleague_id and most
families need pay; Balance needs contractHoursForDate, which colleagues
don't have configured at all; Year in Numbers is built from payslips; Crystal
Ball's projection and its own accuracy grading are woven through pay and
contract hours throughout, not a separable schedule-only core. Did You Know
is AI-generated commentary about your own relationship to your data (e.g.
"you've shared exactly one shift with 3 colleagues") rather than a page
that means anything re-pointed at someone else. Building a colleague view
for any of these would mean a mostly-empty page or numbers borrowed from
your own account under someone else's name — worse than not having it.

entries.summary: Real map on Clock Map, a plain-English What's New, and a duplicated weekday fixed
entries.details:
- Clock Map now shows a real interactive map (OpenStreetMap tiles via
  Leaflet), not just the abstract distance scatter — reconsidered the earlier
  decision not to embed one, since the app already sends every fix to Google
  Maps and already lazy-loads SheetJS from a CDN, so "no third-party JS"
  wasn't actually a constraint this page was holding to.
- What's New has a Basic/Descriptive toggle (top right) — Basic shows just
  plain bullet points, Descriptive keeps the full technical write-up.
- Fixed a table showing the weekday twice (e.g. "Tue Tue 17:05") on Check
  Habits and Clock Map.

Details:

The map is lazy-loaded (loadLeafletLib in utils.js, same pattern as the
existing xlsx loader for Import) so nothing but this one page pays for it.
It sits alongside the existing scatter rather than replacing it — the map
gives street context, the scatter gives an exact metre reading that doesn't
depend on eyeballing a zoom level.

What's New: past entries were written as dense technical prose (aimed at
understanding a bug, not skimming a changelog), so Basic mode has nothing to
show beyond the one-line summary for anything before this release — that's
expected, not a bug. Going forward, commit messages will lead with short
"- " bullets for Basic mode, followed by the fuller explanation for
Descriptive, which is what generate-changelog.js's existing "- " convention
already half-supported.

The duplicated weekday: `dow` (a weekday name, already supplied by the
server) was being paired with `fmtDayShort(date)`, a client helper that
independently computes the exact same weekday name from the date — so two
tables read "Tue Tue 09/09" instead of "Tue 9 Sep". Added fmtDayMonth() (day
+ short month, no weekday) for pairing next to an already-known weekday, and
switched both affected tables plus the new map's popups to use it.

entries.summary: A check only ever got recorded when the app closed, and often it never closed cleanly
entries.details:
Ed's report after v5.6.2: Check Habits was still showing ~98% "walked in
blind" despite him opening the app before every single shift to clock in.
Root cause was two bugs deeper than the coverage-window fix in v5.6.2:

1. A "check" (a view of Dashboard/Shifts/Calendar/Clock/etc.) is only ever
   turned into a recorded row when it *closes* — via the pagehide or
   visibilitychange browser events. That's fine for an ordinary browsing
   session, but "open the app, tap Clock In, close it" can be over in a few
   seconds, and iOS in particular does not reliably fire pagehide when an app
   is swiped away from the app switcher rather than backgrounded normally —
   so the entire visit, and the one thing this feature exists to measure about
   it, was silently never recorded. Fixed by sending a one-time early "ping"
   ~15s after a view opens if it hasn't closed yet, so a short visit has
   already banked a row before it can be killed outright. Deliberately a
   single ping rather than a repeating one — fragmenting an ordinary longer
   session into a run of 15s rows would have inflated "checks" and "views
   opened" for the sessions that were never the problem. Verified with a
   scripted harness: a 5s visit that used to record nothing now records one
   row at the 15s mark, and a session that continues afterwards still reports
   its real total duration with no double-counting.

2. The Dashboard's own Clock In/Out buttons — the ones actually on screen by
   default, and so probably what's really being used day to day — never
   called into V5Tracker at all, unlike the separate Clock In/Out page. That
   meant no location fix and no explicit clock_in/clock_out event from what is
   likely the primary path. Brought it in line with the dedicated page.

entries.summary: Calendar sync gaps, Hide Money blur gaps, and V5 Check Habits false-nonsensical numbers
entries.details: Batch of bug fixes from an autonomous review pass, all patch-level (no new feature surface): - Google Calendar: bulk shift imports (Rotageek raw import, ICS, CSV) never pushed to Google Calendar, and syncAll/reconcile could create stale duplicate events by upserting from a snapshot that went stale mid-loop. - Hide Money: three raw £ strings on the Dashboard (Next Payday, Month Summary, live pay counter) bypassed the money-blur wrapper entirely, and Payslips leaked "..." as visible text next to the leave badge because fmtCurrency's HTML was placed inside a title="" attribute. - V5 Check Habits: the "all time" view compared checks against every shift ever logged, including years before the V5 tracking feature existed to record a check — producing a false ~100% "walked in blind" figure. Bounded the coverage window to when tracking actually started. - V5 Clock Map: renamed the confusingly-named "Fixes relative to the store" section to "Distance from the store", and documented why it stays a plain scatter rather than becoming a tile map (would leak clock-in GPS coordinates to a third-party tile server on every load, and be the app's first external JS dependency, for no real gain over what the scatter already shows). - Standardized employee-selector labelling ("Employee:") across Insights and Shift DNA. Full reasoning and verification detail is in the individual commits on the auto-fixes-2026-09-09 branch this squashes.

entries.summary: Creating a shift without a break no longer assumes 30 minutes
entries.details:
POST /api/shifts defaulted break_scheduled_minutes to a flat 30, so any
shift created without an explicit break lost half an hour of paid time
regardless of its length — a 4-hour shift entitled to no break at all came
out as 3.50h. It now defaults to autoBreakMinutes() for those hours, the
same policy as everywhere else.

The browser form always sends a break, so this only ever hit API callers
and imports, which is why it went unnoticed.

Found by booting the app and creating the real 9-15 Feb week through the
API: 15:00-19:00 came back as 3.5h paid instead of 4.00h. Syntax checks and
unit tests had all passed.

Lockfile version field was still on 2.1.9; npm brought it in line. No
dependency changes.

entries.summary: Data Doctor flags weeks that came out under contract
entries.details:
Every wrong number chased this week showed up first as a week under the
weekly contract, and nothing in the app said so — it had to be spotted by
reading Rotageek's totals against the app's by eye.

Ed is rostered at or above contract essentially always, and payroll only
docks for sickness, which it pays straight back. That makes a completed
week landing short a reliable sign the data is wrong rather than the week:
a shift that never imported, or a break deducted that was never taken. The
9-15 Feb week read 19.50h for exactly that reason.

Leave and sickness both count towards the contract, so neither makes a week
short. Leave counts by its real hours rather than by day — a 'day_off'
carries none, and treating it as a full day would have hidden a genuine
shortfall. Weeks still in progress are skipped.

Also fixed a duplicate here: the Data Doctor had its own hand-copied break
policy, which kept the old strict-> boundary and would now report every
4h30 shift as a discrepancy that isn't. It calls autoBreakMinutes.

Two test files under test/, both run by npm test.

entries.summary: Break policy was wrong at 4h30, in six different places
entries.details:
A shift of exactly 4h30 carries 15 minutes of unpaid break in Rotageek's
journal. autoBreakMinutes used a strict >, returned 0, and so counted every
such shift 0.25h longer than it was. Three are visible in the data alone —
16 Feb, 14 Aug and 16 Sep 2026 — which is why the week of 16 Feb read
21.25h against Rotageek's own total of 21 hrs.

The boundaries are deliberately not consistent with each other. 4h30 is
inclusive, matching the company's "4.5 hours or more"; 6h is exclusive,
matching the Working Time Regulations entitlement for working *more than*
six hours. 19 Aug 2026 is exactly 6h00 and carries 15m, not 30m, while
6h15 carries 30m. Making them agree looks like a tidy-up and silently
changes pay, so there is now a test that fails if anyone does.

The policy was written out six times — db.js, the client break preview, the
Rotageek fallback, the Data Doctor, a SQL CASE in v3/helpers, and
working-with.js — and had already drifted into two different rules:
working-with.js was inclusive at 4h30 (right, by accident) but had no 45m
tier at all. They now all defer to db.js, or carry a comment saying why
they cannot.

test/break-policy.test.js checks all six-way agreement against 29 real
shifts with Rotageek's own break figures. `npm test` runs it. It caught my
first attempt at this fix, which made 6h inclusive too and broke 19 Aug.

Existing rows are untouched: this changes what the app computes for new and
re-checked shifts, not what is already stored. The break audit will now
list affected past shifts as discrepancies so they can be reviewed rather
than silently rewritten — and a break someone deliberately set can be
pinned with the v5.2.0 lock so the audit leaves it alone.

entries.summary: A shift can be marked off sick, and stops counting as worked
entries.details:
Ed's January sick week was stored as four ordinary completed shifts, so the
app counted 20 hours he was at home for as hours worked. There was no way
to say "rostered, but I wasn't there".

New absence_type on shifts, NULL for the normal case. Marked 'sick' the
hours still count towards the contract but no longer count as worked, which
is exactly how payroll treats them: the basic is docked by working day
(Jan 2026: £1,130.14 x 5/21 = £269.08) and handed straight back as company
sick pay £239.39 plus SSP £29.69 — the same £269.08, netting to zero. You
were contracted and paid for the day; you simply didn't work it.

That split falls out of keeping completed at 0: scheduled_hours already
counts every rostered shift, hours_worked already counts completed ones,
and break stats already ignore anything not completed — so a sick day lands
on the right side of each without special-casing the sums. What did need
guarding is everything that would quietly tick it off again: clock-out
auto-complete now skips absences, bulk-complete skips them, and the single
complete endpoint refuses with a message rather than silently flipping it.

Shown as its own thing rather than as a shift still waiting to be done — a
SICK tag and 🤒 in place of the tick, an hours-off-sick stat card, and a
per-week total beside the leave one. The monthly API returns sick_hours and
sick_count so the other views can use them.

entries.summary: Contracted HOURS go pro-rata; 52/12 stays for pay
entries.details:
52/12 is right for basic pay and wrong for hours, and the app used it for
both. Payroll annualises: Basic Salary is an identical twelfth every month
across all 21 payslips, whether the month is 28 days or 31. But 52/12 asks
4.333 weeks of rota from every month, and a 28-day February contains 4.000.
February therefore read ~6.67h under contract every year however the rota
fell, and 31-day months ~1.90h over — an artefact of the yardstick, not the
hours worked. Feb 2026 showed 11.67h under while payroll paid 1.25h of
additional hours for the same month.

Contracted hours are now weekly x days_in_month / 7, so February asks for
80.00h and August 88.57h. Feb 2026 goes from -11.67h to -5.00h, and the
remainder is real: Sun 1 Feb delivered nothing, being the tail of the week
off sick. Sep goes from -1.92h to -0.96h. The annual total is unchanged to
within 3h — the hours are redistributed, not invented. Leap years fall out
of the date maths rather than needing a case.

Same fix in the streaks endpoint, where the old basis broke the
on-contract streak every February for a reason unrelated to the rota.

Pay is untouched: payslips.js and v3/payAudit.js still compute expected
basic as weekly x 52/12 x rate, which is what payroll pays and what "Paid
vs Est." needs to compare against.

Also confirmed correct while checking, so left alone: bank holidays really
are worth 2x. Payroll pays the hours normally and adds a separate
"Bank Holiday Hrs (x1)" premium line, so the app's single 2x per shift
reaches the same total.

entries.summary: A break can be locked so nothing puts it back
entries.details:
"Keep this break exactly as set" on the shift form. The policy thresholds
in autoBreakMinutes are the usual case, not the only one — a manager can
drop the break so you finish earlier — and three separate paths would put
it back, each taking the shift's paid hours down with it: Recalculate All
(fixed in 5.1.9), the break audit, and the Rotageek journal sync. All
three now leave a locked break alone, and the audit stops listing it as a
discrepancy at all, since offering to correct the deliberate thing is how
it gets corrected by accident.

This is what put the week of 9 Feb at 19.50h against a 20h contract and
made a normal week read as a shortfall.

New break_locked column, defaulting to 0, so nothing changes for existing
shifts until the box is ticked.

entries.summary: Stop Recalculate All rewriting deliberate break changes
entries.details:
Recalculate All recomputed break_scheduled_minutes from the policy
thresholds for every shift in the database and wrote it back, discarding
whatever was stored. A break a manager had actually removed — so Ed could
go home earlier — got silently added back, which took that shift's paid
hours down with it and dropped the week from 20.00h to 19.50h, reading as
a genuine shortfall against contract. No audit row was written, so there
was nothing to explain why a settled past week had changed.

It now re-derives only the values that follow from what is stored:
hours_worked, hours_paid, calculated_pay and the bank-holiday catch-up.
The stored break is taken as given, falling back to the policy figure
only where a shift has none at all.

Note the endpoint already protected is_bank_holiday this way — "only ever
adds the flag, never removes a manually-set one" — so a manual override
was understood to be worth keeping; the break just never got the same
guard. The other two paths that touch breaks were already careful: the
Rotageek sync takes the employer's journal as authoritative but skips
completed shifts and logs, and the break audit reports discrepancies
first and only applies the ones chosen. Correcting breaks to policy is
that audit's job, and it remains the way to do it.

entries.summary: Hide Money toggle, for looking at the rota in public
entries.details:
A sidebar switch by the version readout that blurs every money amount on
screen and stays that way until switched back — the rota is often open
where someone else can see it, and shifts and hours are not the private
part of it.

fmtCurrency now wraps its output in a .money span, so one CSS rule covers
all 251 call sites and nothing has to know which of its numbers are
money. The blur is set in em rather than px so it scales with the text:
a 22px stat value and an 11px table cell both end up equally unreadable
rather than one of them staying legible.

The state lives in an attribute on <html> plus localStorage, so it
survives view re-renders and reloads without any view having to
participate, and toggling it redraws nothing.

fmtCurrencyPlain is the unwrapped version, for the one place the result
goes somewhere markup can't — a title attribute on the forecast bar.
Audited the rest first: no money reaches a canvas, an SVG text node,
textContent, a toast or an export, so those cannot show the markup.

entries.summary: Shifts tracks the contract by week; payslips keep the 52/12 maths
entries.details:
The Shifts tab summarised a calendar month directly above a table grouped
into whole Mon-Sun weeks, so the two could never be reconciled by hand.
September 2026 made the gap plain: every week was on or over contract
(+1.25, 0, +5.25, 0, +3.00 = +9.50h) while the month read 1.92h under.
Both were arithmetically right. The month ends on a Wednesday and 20 of
that last week's 23 hours land in October, so September gave away 24.75h
of hours at its boundaries and only got 14.29h of contract back — and
52/12 asks for a 30.44-day month where September has 30, worth another
0.95h. Nothing was wrong and there was no way to see that from the page.

Contract tracking now runs on the weeks actually shown, in a strip
between the cards and the table: total scheduled vs the sum of those
weeks' contracts, which by construction equals the week rows underneath
it. The month-vs-payroll comparison is not duplicated here any more —
Payslips has owned it all along in Hours vs Contract, in plain English
and next to the payslip it exists to be checked against.

The remaining stat cards stay calendar-month and are unchanged: this
month's shifts, hours, pay and distance. Only the contract question
moved, because only that one is answered in weeks.

weekSummaries() is now the single source for both the strip and the
table's week headers. They computed the same week two different ways
before — the header from start/end minus the scheduled break, the cards
from hours_worked — which is how a skipped break put 1.25h between two
figures for the same days.

entries.summary: An under-contract month was missing its minus sign
entries.details:
The Shifts tab's Over/Under card prefixed '+' when positive and an empty
string when negative, so 84.75h against an 86.67h contract rendered as
"1.92h" — identical to being 1.92h over, with only the red colour to
tell them apart, while the two cards beside it plainly showed Hours
below Contracted. Now signed, and the hint says "Under contract" or
"Over contract" in words. The Reports tab has always rendered this
correctly; this brings the Shifts tab in line.

Distance's hint said "Completed shifts only" and the card doesn't —
it sums every shift in the month, done or not. Hint corrected to match.

Also tooltipped the per-week contracted figure. Weekly over/unders don't
sum to the monthly one and are not supposed to: a week straddling a
month boundary is counted whole against a whole week's contract, so
September's five week-rows carry 100h of contract where the month
itself is 52/12 x 20 = 86.67h.

entries.summary: Shifts tab hours were leaking across the month boundary
entries.details:
Hours (Month) and Over/Under on the Shifts tab summed shifts spilling
into the adjacent month too. this.shifts intentionally carries a day or
two from August/October so a week straddling the 1st can render as one
row in the table, but renderStats() never filtered that back out before
totalling — so the month's stats counted more days than the calendar
month actually has, against a Contracted figure that's strictly this
month's. Also switched to hours_paid (was hours_worked, which
overstates by ~1 break's worth whenever a break was worked through
instead of taken) and added leave into the month total, matching how
the Monthly Reports tab already computes both.

Added a one-line hint under every stat card explaining what it adds up
(e.g. "Hours (Month)" now says what's included) since the mismatch
between this tab's numbers and the weekly rows underneath it was hard
to reason about without knowing the scope of each figure.

entries.summary: Contract hours change too, not just get set
entries.details:
Bumping someone's hours used to overwrite a single number on the colleague,
which silently re-priced every past week's overtime and cover-finder maths
along with the future ones. Contract hours are now dated the same way role
pay already is: Manage People logs each change with an effective-from date,
and every read (fatigue audit, cover finder, team calendar, weekly-hours
stats) looks up whichever entry was in force for the week in question.

entries.summary: V5 ships under its own major version
entries.details:
The V5.0 feature set landed in 4.25.0, following the convention that a feature
set's name and the app version are separate things (the V3.0 set shipped in
3.4.0). Ed would rather they line up when a set is big enough to be a new
generation, so the app version moves to 5.0.0 to match.

Version only — no behaviour change. package.json is the single source: the
sidebar readout and every ?v= asset token derive from it, so this also busts
the asset cache for the V5 files that shipped in the previous commit.

entries.summary: The app starts watching itself
entries.details:
V5.0 — usage analytics. Five new views behind one sidebar entry, in the same
shape as the V3 set: a self-contained v5/ router mounted with one line, a
client registry app.js resolves rather than naming each view.

  App Usage      opens, session length, time of day, streaks, trend
  Screen Time    per-view dwell and opens, entry/exit screens, common routes
  Check Habits   how far ahead you check the rota, measured against the rota
  Clock Map      GPS at clock-in/out, labelled against named places
  Data & Privacy the switches, the row counts to check them, and delete buttons

Location is off by default and the switches are enforced server-side in
v5/ingest.js, so turning it off takes effect on the next request rather than
the next page load — a stale client cannot record a fix. The tracker only gates
whether to *ask* for GPS, to avoid an OS prompt for a feature that is off.

Nothing V5 owns touches an existing table. Clock-in GPS lives in v5_locations
keyed by date rather than as columns on clock_entries, so deleting V5's data
never touches a clock record. The fix is requested in parallel with the
clock-in call so a slow or refused GPS can never delay clocking in.

Also fixes a latent layout bug this exposed: .main-content is a flex item, so
its default min-width:auto meant a wide table dragged the whole page sideways
instead of scrolling inside its own .table-wrapper. min-width:0 lets the scroll
containers work — Settings was overflowing at desktop widths before this too.

entries.summary: Pay belongs to the role, not to fourteen people one at a time
entries.details:
Four real roles — Branch Manager, Assistant Manager, Duty Manager, Store
Assistant — replace the old three-way management/supervisor/floor_staff tier,
and the rate now hangs off the role. Set the store assistant rate once and
every store assistant is costed from it; set the AM salary once and both
assistant managers get it. Managers default to salaried, the shop floor to
hourly, but the pay type is per-rate rather than fixed to the role.

Rates are dated the same way pay_rates already are: a row applies FROM a date
and the newest one on or before a shift's date wins, so a rise doesn't
silently rewrite what last year's shifts cost. Everything that costs a
colleague shift — team metrics, the CSV export — now asks for the rate as of
that shift's own date rather than today's.

Nobody's numbers moved on the upgrade. Each role's opening rate is seeded
from what its people were already on (the most common value), dated 1970 so
it covers all history, and anyone who was on something different keeps their
own figure behind a "paid differently to the rest of this role" tick. That
checkbox is the only thing that now shows the per-person pay fields — the
common case is four numbers in one place instead of fourteen scattered ones.

The old three tiers fold in as supervisor→Duty Manager and
floor_staff→Store Assistant. 'management' covered both BM and AM and nothing
in the data says which is which, so both land on Assistant Manager: there's
one branch manager and it's a one-click fix, where guessing would quietly
mis-cost whoever it picked.

Also here, groundwork for running the V3 features as someone else:
shiftsSource() in v3/helpers.js returns a FROM-clause that makes a
colleague's shifts look exactly like mine — break from the shared policy,
rate from their role as of each date — so the existing module SQL and the
existing paidHours/shiftPay maths carry over without a second data model.
distance_miles is always NULL there on purpose: mileage is a property of my
commute and there is no colleague equivalent to invent.

autoBreakMinutes moved from server.js to db.js, since colleague costing needs
the same policy and two copies of the break thresholds is the last thing pay
maths needs.

entries.summary: On This Day echoes now stay on the date
entries.details:
"Same shift, other years" searched every past shift on any date, matching on
start and end time alone. On a 12:15–18:45 Thursday in September that came
back with the previous October, July, June and November — seven shifts, none
of them this date, all labelled "1 year ago" because a year difference is all
they had in common. The date is the entire premise of the page; matching on
time alone threw it away.

The candidates are now the flashback rows — this calendar date, or the
nearest same weekday, in each previous year — narrowed to the ones whose
start and end are both within 30 minutes of today's. The window is still
there because a slot drifts: 12:15–18:45 and 12:45–18:45 on the same date a
year apart are plainly the same shift, and that pair is what the same
September date actually returns now.

Ordered most recent year first, since they all share a date and closeness
only breaks a tie within one. Heading says which date rule is in force.

entries.summary: Pick an incomplete shift when auto-completing on clock-out
entries.details:
On a split-shift day the shift nearest the clock-out time is often the
morning one that's already done, and choosing it left the afternoon shift
open — the case the auto-complete exists to prevent. Only shifts that aren't
already complete are candidates now.

entries.summary: Read the week off the photo, read the times off the calendar
entries.details:
The rename queue was asking Gemini the wrong question. It sent OLLAMA_PROMPT
— "transcribe every shift on this rota" — and then used one field of the
answer. Any slip anywhere in that transcription came back as invalid JSON and
therefore as "could not read a week range", so a photo that was perfectly
legible failed three times and gave up. It now asks only for the week, as ISO
dates, which is both a far easier question and several times cheaper out of
the same free-tier allowance.

The header parser was the other half of it. resolveWeekDates only understood
"Month DD, YYYY" at the very end of the string. "25 Aug - 31 Aug 2026",
"25/08/2026 - 31/08/2026", "Aug 25 - 31, 2026" and any header without a year
all parsed to null — and null is a 422 that costs an attempt. There's now a
wider net behind it that finds the last date anywhere in the string and fills
in month and year from earlier in it, choosing the year that puts the week
nearest today when none is written down. A failure now quotes what Gemini
actually said, so the queue card can tell "not a rota" from "a format we
don't know".

Tapping a photo opens it. The full-screen zoom/pan viewer has been there
since v4.22.0 but only behind a 26px magnifier button; tapping the card
toggled selection instead. Now the card opens the viewer, a circle in the
corner selects, and once anything is selected tapping anywhere adds to the
selection — so multi-select still works without hitting a small target
repeatedly.

Shift times are readable on a phone again. On a 375px screen a day column is
~44px, and after cell and block padding "11:15" at 12px had 25px to fit into
and was cut in half by overflow:hidden — the one thing the calendar exists to
show, unreadable. Sized to the column that actually exists.

Clocking out marks the shift complete, server-side. It used to happen only in
the browser, after the clock-out call returned, behind a break-length modal:
dismiss that modal, lock the phone or close the tab and the clock entry saved
while the shift stayed open. The server now completes it assuming the
scheduled break, and the client's answer to the break question corrects it if
it differs.

Subscribed calendars can see changes now. The feed is rebuilt from the
database on every request, so a moved shift was always in it — but without
SEQUENCE or LAST-MODIFIED a client is entitled to keep showing the copy it
already imported. Both are now sent, along with no-cache headers. Note that
how often a calendar app re-reads the feed is still its own business: Apple
Calendar can be set to 5 minutes, Google decides for itself and can take a
day.

Delivery weather on the dashboard. On a delivery day the hero card adds the
06:00 forecast at the store alongside the two commute legs — the cages get
unloaded outside whether or not the shift starts at nine.

Electricity vs petrol, side by side. Both sets of car figures were already
stored regardless of which fuel type was selected, so the same mileage can be
costed both ways without changing a setting. Shows both totals, per-mile and
per-shift, which is cheaper and by how much, and the price at which they'd
swap places.

entries.summary: Let the queues wait out the free tier instead of fighting it
entries.details:
No billing, so the answer is patience: keep going until the backlog is done,
however long the free tier makes that take.

Both background queues now share one throttle. They spend the same allowance,
so being told "no" in one is a reason for the other to hold off too —
otherwise they take turns burning a locked-out quota every 30 seconds and
neither finishes. A refusal pauses both for a minute, doubling to fifteen if
it keeps happening, and the first success clears it. Google's own "retry in
644ms" is treated as a floor, not advice: the free tier's window is
per-minute, so obeying it literally walks straight back into the same wall.

The screenshot-import queue had the same bug the rename queue had in v4.20.0
— a rate-limit error still cost that screenshot one of its three attempts —
so it's fixed there too.

Rename batch is 5 a tick (10/min against the free tier's 20), leaving room
for the screenshot queue and anything done by hand.

The queue card now says when it's sitting out a quota window and how long is
left, rather than looking stalled. Photos that genuinely can't be read still
give up after three attempts — retrying those forever would spend the
allowance the readable ones need.

entries.summary: Retry-all for the rename queue, readable quota errors, sticky auto-rename
entries.details:
The rename failures were Gemini's free-tier quota — 20 requests a minute —
which v4.20.0 stopped counting as the photo's fault. Three follow-ons now
that the error is known:

Retry all. A quota outage fails jobs by the hundred and the only way back was
one Retry button per card, which isn't a real option on a phone. The queue
header grows a "↻ Retry all N" button whenever more than one has given up.

Readable errors. Google's version is three sentences and two support URLs;
none of it fits in a 96px card. A quota failure now reads "Gemini quota
reached (20/min on the free tier) — waiting, will retry itself".

The auto-rename toggle is remembered server-side. It kept coming back
unticked on the phone and it persists correctly in every path I could
reproduce, so the local copy is what's being lost — per-browser storage is
exactly the thing that gets cleared out from under you, or is simply a
different browser. It now saves to settings like any other preference, with
localStorage kept as an instant fallback.

entries.summary: Stat cards three across on a phone, not one per row
entries.details:
Below 480px every stat card was forced full width, so Shifts opened with
thirteen of them — thirteen screenfuls of scrolling before the shift table.
They're now auto-filled at a 104px minimum: three across on a normal phone,
two on the narrowest, with smaller labels and values to match. Thirteen cards
go from thirteen rows to five.

The rule needs !important: Reports, Insights and What If set
grid-template-columns inline, and an inline style beats a stylesheet rule
however specific it is. Tablet (2-up) and desktop are untouched.

entries.summary: Fix the month calendar's columns on a phone
entries.details:
Two things had the grid coming apart at phone width:

The day-name header spanned the full width while the cells sat in a flex row
next to the 68px weekly-totals column, so the headings were already a slice
of a column out of step with the days underneath them — on a wide screen too,
just less visibly.

And `1fr` is `minmax(auto, 1fr)`: a cell can't be narrower than its own
min-content, and the shift chips are `white-space: nowrap`. So every column
holding a shift grew to fit "12:15 – 18:45" (~105px), the row overflowed the
screen with Saturday and Sunday off the right-hand edge, and September's
Monday column — which has no shifts at all — collapsed to a 20px sliver.

Columns are now minmax(0, 1fr), the header reserves the totals gutter, and at
phone width the times stack (start over end, no dash) instead of wrapping
into three lines around the dash.

entries.summary: Rearrangeable sidebar, and a rename queue that waits out a busy API
entries.details:
Sidebar: "✏️ Edit menu" at the bottom turns the nav into an editor — drag ⠿
to move any tab, make your own groups (＋ Group), rename or delete them
(deleting keeps the tabs, they move back out to the top level), and Reset
puts it all back. Saved in settings so the layout follows you between the
phone and the desktop. The default layout is still index.html's markup, read
at boot, so a tab added later appears on its own instead of being invisible
to a saved layout.

Rename queue: a quota, rate-limit or overload error from Gemini says nothing
about the photo it happened on, but it still burned one of that photo's
three attempts — three ticks 30s apart and a whole queued batch could be
marked failed without a single image having been looked at. Those errors now
leave the attempt count alone, end the tick (whatever is throttling us
applies to everything behind it too), and show as "Waiting to retry — ..." on
the card. The queue also splits waiting from failed by attempts rather than
by "has an error at all".

entries.summary: Photo viewer, correct Next In day labels, honest clock-out
entries.details:
Photo Library: tap 🔍 on any photo to open it full-screen, with pinch /
wheel / +- zoom up to 8x, drag to pan, swipe or arrows between photos, and
double-tap to jump to 250%. The per-photo buttons no longer hide behind
:hover on touch devices, where they were unreachable.

Dashboard "Next In": after the evening rollover cutoff the roster window
starts at tomorrow, but the headings still said "Today"/"Tomorrow" — so at
20:00 on a Wednesday it listed Thursday's shifts under TODAY. The window is
unchanged; only the labels now follow the real calendar date.

Clock out: marking the linked shift complete could silently not happen —
no shift on today's rota, the break question dismissed, or the
bulk-complete request failing (which reported "clock out failed" instead).
Each case now says what happened, on both the dashboard and the Clock
In/Out page.

Rename queue: failed jobs show the error on the card instead of only in a
title tooltip, which a phone can't show.

entries.summary: Route large AI-rename selections through the background queue
entries.details:
Selecting a large batch of unrenamed photos (e.g. "Select All" on hundreds)
and clicking "AI Rename" ran a synchronous loop of Gemini calls in the
browser tab -- the exact problem already fixed for uploads, just reachable
from a different button. Selections over 10 photos now get queued via the
new POST /photo-library/rename-queue/bulk endpoint and processed by the same
background loop as auto-rename-on-upload, so closing the tab or losing
connection mid-batch no longer throws away progress. Small selections (<=10)
still rename immediately, since that's fast enough to just wait for.

entries.summary: Make the rename queue's activity visible
entries.details:
The rename queue had no filename captions and gave no confirmation when a
photo finished renaming, so it looked identical whether it was working or
stalled. Added filenames under each queued thumbnail, a header line ("2
waiting, 1 failed"), and a toast when photos finish renaming.

entries.summary: Rename queue for Photo Library, queue fixes
entries.details:
- Team Upload's Processing Queue no longer shows completed screenshots --
  finished items (imported or needing review) belong in Recent Imports, not
  a queue of in-flight work.
- "Auto-rename with AI on upload" (Photo Library) now uses the same
  background-queue approach as the screenshot importer instead of looping
  Gemini calls synchronously in the upload request -- same reliability risk,
  same fix. A new "Rename queue" card shows waiting/failed thumbnails with a
  Retry button; manual "AI Rename" on selected photos stays synchronous since
  that's a PC-driven, wait-for-it action.
- The auto-rename checkbox now persists via localStorage instead of
  resetting to unchecked on every re-render/navigation.
- team-upload and photo-library are now included in the router's
  outgoing-view cleanup, so their background pollers actually stop when you
  navigate away instead of running indefinitely.

entries.summary: Visual screenshot processing queue
entries.details:
Replaced the buried one-line status text with a proper thumbnail grid card
("Processing Queue") on the Team Upload page, always visible regardless of
which import tab is active. Each queued screenshot shows as a thumbnail with
a status badge: waiting, failed (with a Retry button and the actual error on
hover), or done (with either an inserted-shift count or a "N to review"
badge that scrolls to and opens the matching Recent Imports row). Backing
GET /colleagues/screenshot-queue now also returns recently-finished items
with their outcome, not just pending/failed.

entries.summary: Background processing queue for screenshot imports
entries.details:
Uploading a screenshot from a phone ran upload + Gemini read + import as one
HTTP request, so a slow Gemini call or the tab getting backgrounded
mid-request (trivial to do on mobile) killed the whole thing with a bare
"Failed to fetch" and nothing saved. The Auto Import (AI) panel now just
uploads the raw file -- fast, small, hard to fail -- into the Photo Library
with queued_for_import=1; a server-side loop (working-with.js) picks up
unprocessed screenshots every 30s, reads them with Gemini, and runs them
through the same import pipeline as manual JSON import, independent of the
phone staying connected. Team Upload shows queue progress and any errors
(with a Retry button) via the new GET/POST /colleagues/screenshot-queue
endpoints. Also added a timeout to the Gemini vision call itself (previously
unbounded, unlike the text path) so one stuck request can't stall the queue.

entries.summary: Cross-device conflict review for team screenshot imports
entries.details:
Screenshot imports could only be reviewed for conflicts on whichever device
did the upload -- awkward on a phone's small screen, and if you left without
resolving them the conflicts just vanished (only ever held in that browser
tab's memory). Import batches now persist their pending conflicts + original
schedule JSON server-side, so any device can pick them up: Recent Imports on
the Team Upload page shows a "Review (N)" button for batches with unresolved
conflicts, opening the same resolve/skip/replace table inline. The Auto
Import (AI) panel also imports immediately after Gemini reads a screenshot
instead of waiting for a manual Import tap, and the page polls for new
imports every 20s so a phone upload shows up on the PC without a refresh.

entries.summary: Rotageek session keep-alive heartbeat
entries.details:
Autosync only touched the Rotageek session once per (default 1h) interval,
so a session cookie with a shorter inactivity TTL could go stale between
runs -- the Import page kept showing "Connected" with no indication sync
had quietly stopped working. Added a 20-minute keep-alive heartbeat that
reuses the existing auth-refresh chain (password re-auth, then bearer
fallback) to touch the session more often than it can expire, and clears
the stale session_expired flag once a request succeeds again. The Import
page also now re-polls status every 60s while the Rotageek tab is open.

entries.summary: Pay-accuracy audit — breaks are unpaid, one contracted-hours rule, import and overnight fixes
entries.details:
An audit of the pay-critical paths after the leave bug, checked against all
336 shifts and 22 payslips on record rather than by reading alone.

BREAKS ARE NEVER PAID (confirmed with Ed). The code already had this right —
`hours_paid` always deducts the scheduled break — but two things around it
disagreed, both in the direction of inventing money:

- The monthly report summed `hours_worked`, which keeps the time back when a
  break is worked through. Across the dataset that overstated hours by 22.67h,
  so Hours vs Contract and Reports credited ~23 hours of unpaid time towards
  the contract. Both totals now sum `hours_paid`.

- Reports showed "Unused break pay — extra earned on skipped breaks", £385.20
  of money that does not exist, and the README claimed the app "adds the
  scheduled break minutes back as paid time". The figure is now reported as
  what it is: unpaid time worked. `break_unused_pay` stays in the API response
  as a constant 0 rather than being removed outright, so an older cached
  client can't crash on it.

  The README now documents `hours_paid` vs `hours_worked` explicitly, since
  the whole class of error came from those two being used interchangeably.

ONE CONTRACTED-HOURS RULE. Hours vs Contract, Reports and the Shifts tab used
weekly x Mon-Fri days / 5; Pay Audit used weekly x 52/12. The second is what
payroll uses — basic pay of £1168.48 is exactly 20 x 52/12 x £13.48 — and the
first swung the target between 80h and 92h for an unchanging 20h contract,
overstating the year by 3.96h. It was also Mon-Fri weighted on a rota that is
38% weekends, the same wrong assumption behind the leave bug. Everything now
uses 52/12, a flat 86.67h. `workingDaysInMonth` had no callers left and is
gone.

CSV AND ICS IMPORT IGNORED THE BREAK POLICY. `parseInt(x, 10) || 30` turned a
legitimate zero into 30 minutes, so importing a 4-hour shift — entitled to no
break — silently lost half an hour of pay. Both paths now fall back to
`autoBreakMinutes()` for the shift's length, and honour an explicit 0.

THE WEEKLY REPORT COULD NOT COUNT AN OVERNIGHT SHIFT. `calcHours` lacked the
midnight wrap that `db.js` and `v3/helpers.js` both have, so a 22:00-06:00
shift scored zero hours. Latent — there are none on record — and verified
fixed by inserting one: it now contributes 7.25h where it previously
contributed nothing.

Checked and found clean, worth recording: `break_scheduled_minutes` matches
the documented policy on all 336 shifts (which is why Ed's half-remembered
4h/5.5h boundaries were not adopted over the saved 4h30/6h ones — real
Rotageek data does not fit a wrong policy perfectly); every shift's stored
rate matches the pay_rates table; all three Monday-key implementations agree;
and only one place still buckets a date range by start date, using an OR
across both ends, which is harmless.

April 2026 across the two fixes: 88h contracted / 65.75h logged reads as
86.67h contracted / 62.25h paid + 37.85h leave = 13.43h over.

entries.summary: Drop the now-unused callGeminiVision export
entries.details:
Left behind by v4.12.0. The payslip photo import was the only thing outside
working-with.js that called it; everything still reading an image with Gemini —
the team screenshot import, the two extract routes, the photo-library AI rename
— sits in that file and calls it directly. The text counterpart stays exported,
since v3/didYouKnow.js uses it.

Nothing else was orphaned by the removal: multer is gone from server.js but is
still used by working-with.js and payslipFiles.js, and the Gemini API key and
model settings still drive the team screenshot import, whose Settings blurb
already describes only that.

entries.summary: Remove the payslip photo import
entries.details:
It earned its place when a payslip meant typing twenty figures. It doesn't now:
v4.11.0 works out basic pay, both pairs of hourly extras, tax, NI and every
total from the month and a couple of quantities, and v4.11.1 keeps the original
PDF itself. Reading a photo with an AI and then checking every figure it
returned is more work than the two numbers the form now actually needs, and it
was one more thing that could quietly put a wrong figure in a saved payslip.

Gone: the 📷 Import from Photo button and its hidden file input, the
_importPayslipPhoto handler, API.extractPayslipPhoto, and the server's
POST /api/payslips/import-photo along with the 60-line PAYSLIP_PROMPT and the
multer instance behind it. server.js no longer imports callGeminiVision, which
that route was its only user of — the function itself stays in working-with.js,
where the team screenshot import and the photo-library AI rename still use it.
Nothing else referenced any of it.

Also corrected while in the README: the schema table described photo_folders /
photo_files as "payslip photo storage", which they never were — they hold the
rota screenshots. They are listed properly now, next to payslip_files, and the
payslip-document endpoints added in v4.11.1 are documented.

Verified in the running app: the toolbar is just "+ Add Payslip", the page loads
with no console errors and no failed requests, the form and the documents card
both still work, and POST /api/payslips/import-photo now returns 404.

entries.summary: Keep the original payslip PDFs — a Payslip Documents section that stores files and reads nothing
entries.details:
Somewhere to put the actual payslip, so the real document is safe rather than
only the figures typed off it. Deliberately inert: nothing reads these files,
nothing extracts from them, and no figure anywhere on the Payslips page comes
from one. The Gemini photo import at the top of the view is the thing that reads
a payslip and it stores nothing — the two never meet.

- New Payslip Documents card at the bottom of the Payslips view: pick a month,
  choose files or drag them onto the box, with an optional note. The list shows
  month, name, size and upload time; each row opens in a new tab, saves a copy,
  or can be retagged, renamed and deleted. Documents follow the year selector at
  the top of the page, and a line says how many are filed under other years so
  an empty list never reads as "nothing was ever uploaded".

- PDFs and images only, 25MB and 20 files a go. Anything else is refused by name
  rather than silently dropped.

- Storage follows the photo library's split, for the same reason: metadata in a
  new payslip_files table, the file itself on disk under
  DATA_DIR/payslip-files/<month>/. Keeping PDFs in the database would bloat the
  file that gets snapshotted nightly. Retagging a document's month moves the file
  between month directories so disk and database stay in agreement, and a
  half-finished upload cleans up after itself rather than leaving files on disk
  that no row points at.

- The flip side of that choice is stated where it matters — in the card, and in
  the README's backup section: uploaded files ride on whatever backs up the data
  volume, because the nightly GitHub backup carries rota.db alone. That already
  applied to the rota screenshots in photo-library and was nowhere in the docs.

Server-side lives in its own root-level payslipFiles.js router, mounted like the
others; root-level .js is already copied by the Dockerfile, so no image change.

Verified against a copy of the live database in the running app: a PDF uploaded
through the form comes back byte-identical from the download endpoint (387
bytes in, 387 out, %PDF header intact), served inline as application/pdf and as
an attachment with ?download=1. Dropping a file on the box files it under the
selected month. Retagging July to June moved the file on disk and the download
still works. Deleting removes both the row and the file. A .txt is refused with
"Only PDFs and images can be stored — notes.txt is neither", and a malformed
month with "A month (YYYY-MM) is required".

entries.summary: Autofill the rest of the payslip form — hourly extras, tax, NI and every total
entries.details:
v4.9.0 filled in Basic Salary and this month's Additional Hours. This does the
same for everything else the app can work out, so entering a payslip is mostly
checking figures rather than typing them. As before, each suggestion was picked
by measuring against all 22 recorded payslips, and as before the obvious formula
lost more than once.

- Additional Hours (prev month) and both Bank Holiday Hours boxes now derive
  their £ from the hours, like this month's already did. The rate is the one in
  force for the month the hours were WORKED, not the month they're paid in:
  April 2026's previous-month hours were paid at March's £13.04, not April's new
  £13.48. Using the payslip's own rate is exact on 16 of 17 and misses that
  month by £1.98; using the worked month's rate is exact on all 17, and on all 5
  payslips with bank holiday hours.

- NI is 8% of gross above the £1,048 monthly primary threshold. Exact on 21 of
  22, including all nine months under the threshold, where it correctly comes to
  nothing. The miss is Nov 2025, a penny over.

- Tax is cumulative PAYE: 20% of everything earned since 6 April above the free
  pay the code allows by this point in the year, less the tax already deducted
  in it. The code is fitted rather than assumed, and that mattered twice —
  2025/26 actually ran on 1240L, so assuming the standard 1257L would have been
  £11.20 out in July 2025; and carrying the fitted code across April would have
  been wrong too, HMRC having put it back to 1257L for 2026/27. So each tax year
  is fitted from its own payslips (one taxed month pins the code to a pound or
  two of allowance, two pin it exactly) and falls back to the standard code
  until one of them has tax on it. Right on 21 of 22 — the miss is July 2025,
  the first taxed month of a year, where there was nothing yet to fit to.

- Total Gross, Total Deductions, Net Payment and the four YTD boxes no longer
  wait for the Auto-calculate button: they keep in step as you type, in the
  order the payslip works — lines make the gross, gross makes tax and NI, those
  make the deductions and the net. The buttons remain, and now hand a field you
  had typed in back to the form.

- Sharesave and SIP carry from the previous month's payslip instead of Sharesave
  being hard-coded at £250 — including whether the section is switched on at
  all, so a new payslip starts with the standing items the last one had. SIP
  stopped in June 2026, so August correctly starts without it.

- Fixed: Taxable and NI'able YTD were subtracting the SIP contribution from a
  gross that already had it taken off — SIP is a negative payment line, so it
  comes off in the total above. The May 2026 payslip settles it, showing taxable
  YTD £2,753.06, exactly the two months' gross. The tax estimate above depends
  on getting this right.

- Not done: Payment Date. Three recorded dates, no rule that fits all three
  (Fri 29 May, Mon 29 Jun, Thu 30 Jul), and the app's existing payday rule —
  most common day, pulled back off a weekend — gets two of the three. A wrong
  date here would feed back into the payday countdown, which infers the day from
  these very dates, so it's better left empty.

Everything stays editable, on the same rule as v4.9.0: a field is only written
while the form still owns it, and typing in it hands it over for good. Anything
that already had a value on open — every field of a saved payslip, or whatever
the photo import read — counts as typed from the start, so editing a payslip
never rewrites what payroll actually paid. Clearing a field by hand now leaves
it cleared, which it didn't before. Each filled field still explains itself
underneath: "8% of the £258.65 above the £1,048 monthly threshold", "8 x £13.48
(July's rate)", "cumulative PAYE on code 1240L, the code that matches the tax on
your earlier payslips this tax year".

Verified in the running app against a copy of the live database. Re-entering the
July 2026 payslip from scratch reproduces it to the penny — 0.5 hrs, 0.5 prev
hrs, the £65.54 leave adjustment and the £22.89 SIP proceeds typed in, and gross
£1,270.39, tax £44.40, NI £17.79, deductions £312.19 and net £958.20 all fall
out. Dec 2025 does the same on the 1240L year once its basic salary is corrected
by hand (Nov 2025's 14->20h transition is one of the three months v4.9.0 already
documents as beyond any formula). Hand-entered figures survive month and hours
changes; a saved payslip opens untouched and stays untouched.

entries.summary: One rule for leave hours, instead of three — holidays no longer read as shortfalls
entries.details:
Reported as "Hours vs Contract doesn't include holiday hours". It didn't, but
that was the smaller half of the problem.

The monthly report grouped leave with strftime('%Y-%m', start_date), so an
entry was booked entirely to the month it began in. A holiday running
30 Mar → 11 Apr counted wholly as March, and April — where nine of its days
actually fell — showed 22.25h under contract and an implied £299.93 missing.
Five of the eleven annual-leave entries on record cross a month boundary, and
the same applied at year boundaries, since the query also filtered on the
start date's year.

Underneath that, three places each spread a leave entry across its days their
own way:

  server.js weekly (Insights)   over Mon–Fri working days
  v3/overtime.js                over every calendar day
  server.js monthly report      not at all

All three now call leaveHours.js. V3's rule won, and the reasoning was already
written down in its docblock: this rota trades seven days and rotates across
all of them. Measured over the last twelve months 38% of shifts fall on a
weekend and Saturday is the single biggest day by hours, so confining leave to
weekdays would pile it onto days often not worked — and an entry falling
entirely on a weekend divided by zero and vanished, leaving that week still
reading as a shortfall. Entries are now selected by overlap rather than by
start date, so a range crossing a boundary contributes to both sides.

Hours vs Contract and the Reports monthly table gain a Leave column and
compare logged + leave against contracted, rather than logged alone. Hours vs
Contract also gains a Covered Hrs column so the arithmetic is visible instead
of the numbers just quietly changing, and says which months include leave.

On the live data April 2026 goes from 22.25h under (−£299.93) to 15.60h over,
which matches the 10.5 additional hours actually paid that month. March, June
and August move similarly. The 27 Oct → 2 Nov 2025 entry now splits 10h/4h
across the two months instead of dumping all 14h in October.

Also fixes a display bug the Leave column made obvious: a negative Over/Under
in Reports rendered without its sign, so September's −51.50h read as "51.50h".
Colour was carrying the whole meaning.

Verified against a copy of the live database: monthly, weekly and V3 Overtime
endpoints all agree on leave per period, and both tables render correctly.

entries.summary: Autofill Basic Salary and Additional Hours pay on the payslip form
entries.details:
Both suggestions were picked by measuring against all 22 recorded payslips
rather than assumed, and one of the two obvious formulas turned out to be
the wrong one.

- Additional Hours £ derives from the hours as you type them: qty x the
  hourly rate for that month. Exact on all 21 payslips that had any
  additional hours — not a penny out on any of them.

- Basic Salary is prefilled on open. The obvious formula, contracted x
  52/12 x rate, is what Pay Audit uses to judge a payslip, but it's a poor
  thing to type in: it lands a penny under on most months and 21p under on
  the current rate (1168.27 against the 1168.48 actually paid). Basic is a
  constant that only moves when the rate or contract does, so the better
  predictor is what payroll actually paid last time on the same rate.
  Carrying that forward is exact on 16 of 22, and the three it misses are
  months no formula could get either — a real underpayment in Jan 2025 and
  the 14->20h transition in Nov 2025. The most common prior value is used
  rather than simply the latest, so one odd month doesn't propagate.

  The formula remains the fallback for the first month on a new rate, where
  there is nothing to carry, and says so in the hint.

Everything stays editable. A field is only ever written while it's still
flagged as autofilled; typing in it clears that flag permanently, so a
hand-entered figure survives later changes to the month or the hours. Values
on an existing payslip are never touched when editing. Each prefilled field
explains itself underneath — "what you were paid in 4 previous months on this
rate", "2 x £13.48" — so the number is checkable rather than magic.

Autofill now runs before the YTD auto-calc rather than after, since YTD falls
back to Basic Salary when there's no gross yet; opening August 2026 gives a
YTD gross of £6729.17 instead of £5560.69.

Verified in the running app against a copy of the live database: August 2026
prefills £1168.48, 2 hours gives £26.96 and 10.25 gives £138.17, all three
matching the real payslips; hand-edited values survive month and hours
changes; switching to June 2025 correctly follows the older rate to £791.10.

entries.summary: Keep Settings cards in place when collapsing; token-protect the iCal feed
entries.details:
Two unrelated fixes from using v4.7.0.

Settings cards no longer shuffle when you collapse one. The masonry layout
was CSS multi-column, which re-balances its columns whenever any content
changes height — so collapsing a single card moved every other card on the
page, often to a different column. Sections are now dealt across real column
elements, left to right, and stay dealt. Collapsing a card moves only the
cards below it in its own column; measured on the live page, collapsing one
section left 10 of the 15 exactly where they were, and the other column
untouched.

Column count still follows the width (one below ~950px of content, three
above ~1440px), recomputed on window resize and when a search narrows the
list, so a lone match isn't stranded in column two.

The live calendar subscription can now carry a token:

- /calendar.ics accepts a token from the settings table (ical_token) as well
  as the ICAL_TOKEN env var, settings winning — same precedence as the GitHub
  backup credentials. With neither set the feed is open, exactly as before.

- Export > Live calendar subscription grows a Generate/Remove control, and
  the URL it displays now includes the token. Previously setting ICAL_TOKEN
  did work, but the page still showed a tokenless URL that would 403, so the
  option was effectively unusable.

This is groundwork for the actual blocker, which is not in the app: Cloudflare
Access intercepts the feed and answers with its sign-in page, and a calendar
client can't complete an interactive login. That needs a Bypass policy scoped
to the /calendar.ics path in Cloudflare Zero Trust — documented in the README,
along with why the token matters once that path is public, and the same
treatment for /clock-tap if the NFC tag should work off-network.

Verified: feed returns 200 with no token configured, 403 without or with a
wrong token once one is set, 200 with the right one; generate/remove round
trips from the Export page and updates the displayed URL live.

entries.summary: Make Settings responsive, searchable and collapsible; pin the mobile topbar
entries.details:
Settings was a single 680px column regardless of screen width, with fifteen
sections stacked in it and no way to jump to one. The GitHub offsite backup
in particular was unfindable: it was a sub-block three quarters of the way
down the Backup & Restore card.

- The page now flows sections into as many ~460px columns as fit
  (masonry-style, so a tall card doesn't leave a gap beside it), collapsing
  to one column on mobile. Replaces the hardcoded max-width.

- Every section collapses from its header, with open/closed state keyed on
  the section title in localStorage so it survives reloads. Expand all /
  Collapse all in the toolbar; collapsed, the whole page is a two-column
  index of what's there. Header buttons ("+ Add Rate") don't toggle.

- Search filters sections live, matching visible text plus per-section
  data-search synonyms — so "pat" or "offsite" finds the GitHub card, and
  "wage" finds Pay Rates. Matching sections force-expand and the matching
  field is highlighted. Employment Milestones, which hides itself when
  there's no job start date, stays hidden.

- Offsite Backup (GitHub) is its own top-level section rather than a block
  inside Backup & Restore, with a cross-link from where it used to live.

Also fixes the topbar, which affected every view, not just Settings:

- The burger menu scrolled off the top on mobile. `.main-content` sets
  overflow-x below 860px, which makes it the topbar's nearest scroll
  container — and since it isn't the element that actually scrolls,
  `position: sticky` never engaged. Pinned it with `position: fixed` in the
  same media block that introduces the overflow, offset by the sidebar
  width down to 768px and full-width below that.

- Removed a leftover `.main-content { padding-top: 52px }` on short desktop
  windows (height <= 800px), which left a 52px blank strip above an
  in-flow topbar. The matching height override now sets --topbar-height so
  anything sized off it follows automatically.

Verified at 375, 820, 1400 and 1600px wide, in light and dark mode, against
a copy of the live database.

entries.summary: Add Pay Audit, Tax Check and Data Doctor to V3
entries.details:
Three checking tools rather than three more lenses — each one exists to
answer "is this actually right?" about data the app already holds.

- 🧾 Pay Audit (/api/v3/pay-audit). Hours worked against hours paid, as
  running totals across a tax year so the month-in-arrears timing can't
  hide a gap: late pay closes its own gap next month, genuinely missing
  hours don't.

  The pay model was read off 22 real payslips rather than assumed, and
  the assumption would have been wrong. Basic is contracted weekly hours
  × 52 ÷ 12 × rate, a constant that doesn't move when you work less.
  Additional hours are counted PER WEEK, with no credit for a quiet week
  either side. Totalling weekly excess predicts the additional hours
  actually paid to within 5% (263.75 vs 250.5 across all payslips);
  totalling monthly, where a light week cancels a heavy one, predicts
  174 and is nowhere near. The first implementation used the monthly
  rule and understated what was owed by roughly 90 hours.

  Because the model is good to ~5% and no better, the headline carries a
  proportional margin and only reports a shortfall that clears it. A
  month 0.25h light is not a finding.

- 💷 Tax Check (/api/v3/tax-check). Every payslip against what cumulative
  PAYE should have deducted, with NI checked per period since it works
  the opposite way. A refund through the payroll after a quiet month is
  marked as the system self-correcting rather than flagged as an error.

  The useful part is inverting the arithmetic: while earnings stay in the
  basic band the allowance the payroll is really using can be solved for,
  which turns "£32 more than expected" into "that's a code around 1240L".
  On the 2025/26 data it reports a £32.06 overpayment and an implied
  1240L against the standard 1257L — and the app has a real £32.20 PAYE
  refund recorded for that year, which the check reproduces without
  being told about it. Reuses forecast.js's bands so the two can't drift.

- 🩺 Data Doctor (/api/v3/health-check). Thirteen integrity checks in one
  pass, each finding carrying the actual rows. On the live data it finds
  5 bank holidays left unflagged and paying single time, 87 shifts whose
  stored hours were left behind by an edit, a week that never imported
  and 6 past shifts never completed. Stale-hours rows show the break
  their hours imply next to the break the policy gives, so it's obvious
  which of the two fields went stale. Read-only throughout — it points,
  and Shifts/the break audit/Recalculate do the changing.

Also documents the break policy in the README, which the Data Doctor
depends on and which was only written down in code.

Verified end to end against a copy of the live database.

entries.summary: Add Leave Optimiser, Cover Finder and Rota Crystal Ball to V3
entries.details:
Three new V3 views, all read-only against existing tables and mounted the
usual way — one entry each in v3/index.js FEATURES, one client file, no
router changes.

- 🏖️ Leave Optimiser (/api/v3/leave-planner). Ranks every possible leave
  booking by days off gained per day booked, so the ones that bridge two
  rest weekends float to the top. The rota only runs a fortnight out, so
  days past the last rostered shift are classed from your own weekday
  pattern and labelled as predictions rather than quietly mixed in with
  the published rota. Flags a rostered bank holiday inside a plan, since
  booking leave there gives up the double time as well as the day.
  Near-identical plans are collapsed — shifting a break by one day scores
  almost the same, and the raw ranking was a dozen copies of one fortnight.

- 🔁 Cover Finder (/api/v3/cover-finder). For any upcoming shift, ranks the
  team on whether they're free that day, how often they work that slot,
  what room they have left under contract that week and how recently
  they've been on the rota, with the reasoning shown next to each score.
  Also lists shifts of theirs you're free for, so it can be a swap rather
  than a favour. Rates are measured over the last year only — over all
  time they went stale and, against a one-year denominator, produced
  weekday percentages above 100.

- 🔮 Rota Crystal Ball (/api/v3/crystal-ball). Projects an unpublished week.
  The model was picked by measuring: backtested over 26 real weeks, a
  16-week weekday rate blended 35/65 with the last known week scores 70%
  against the 58% you'd get by simply assuming you work every day, and
  that comparison is reported in the UI. Exact start times are much
  weaker (24% within an hour) so the view leads with the half of the day
  instead and says so. Where the last-week term flips a call, the card
  explains that rather than just showing a number that contradicts the
  history underneath it.

Verified end to end against a copy of the live database.

entries.summary: Configure GitHub offsite backup from Settings instead of env vars only
entries.details:
Adds repo/token/branch/folder fields under Settings > Backup & Restore,
backed by new GET/POST/DELETE /api/db-backups/github-settings endpoints.
Values are stored in the settings table (token never echoed back) and
take priority over the matching GITHUB_BACKUP_* env var, so it can be
configured without editing docker-compose.yml or restarting.

entries.summary: Add optional GitHub offsite backup for nightly DB snapshots
entries.details:
Pushes each nightly SQLite backup to a GitHub repo via env-configured
PAT (GITHUB_BACKUP_REPO/TOKEN/BRANCH/PATH), mirroring the existing
14-file local retention. Settings page shows configured/unconfigured
status.

entries.summary: Fix bulk time-edit failing entirely on one UNIQUE-constraint collision
entries.details:
The bulk-set-time endpoint ran a single UPDATE across every selected id —
if any one shift's new time collided with the (colleague_id, date,
start_time) unique index (that colleague already has another shift the
same day at the new time), SQLite aborted the whole statement and every
row failed, not just the conflicting one. That's exactly the kind of
messy pre-existing data this bulk action tends to get used to fix.

Now applies row by row inside a transaction: a collision skips just that
row, everything else still goes through, and the skipped shifts are
reported back by name/date instead of a raw SQLite error.

entries.summary: Add bulk time-edit to Team Calendar search results
entries.details:
Search results now have the same checkbox multi-select the Person View
list already had, plus a new "Edit time" bulk action alongside delete —
select every row a mistyped time turned up (e.g. searching "05:45") and
correct them all to the right start/end time in one go, instead of
opening the edit modal on each one individually.

New POST /api/colleague-shifts/bulk-set-time endpoint updates start
and/or end time across a set of ids, restricted to shift_type='shift'
rows so a mixed selection with leave/all_day entries doesn't error.

entries.summary: Fix team import store-conflict bug, add electric car commute cost, add Weather sidebar link, fix Chameleon archetype bias, fix AI fact reasoning leak, add shift echoes to On This Day
entries.details:
- Team screenshot import compared incoming shifts against ALL of a
  colleague's existing shifts for the day regardless of store, so a
  legitimate different-store shift alongside a home-store one got
  flagged as a duplicate/conflict instead of coexisting. Existing-shift
  comparisons are now scoped to the same store context.
- Commute Cost and the Shift Briefing card only ever modelled a petrol
  car (MPG + pence/litre), so an electric car's cost was nonsense.
  Added a fuel type toggle (petrol/electric, miles-per-kWh + pence/kWh)
  shared by both views via a single costPerMileFor() helper — briefing
  previously duplicated a petrol-only calc with its own bug.
- Weather had no sidebar entry, only reachable via V2.0 Features hub.
  Added a direct link under My Rota.
- Shift DNA's archetype picker took the first array-declared match
  among a person's top traits rather than the best one — since variety
  and social both saturate near 100 for anyone on a busy, varied rota,
  almost everyone's top three included that pair and The Chameleon (5th
  in the list) won by default regardless of fit. Now ranks every
  qualifying archetype by its weaker trait's score and picks the
  strongest match.
- The AI fact button could show a truncated reasoning trace instead of
  the finished fact (thinking models spending the token budget on
  reasoning before writing anything visible). Thinking is now disabled
  for 2.5+ models, and a truncated/reasoning-shaped response triggers
  the existing fallback-model retry instead of reaching the user.
- On This Day gets a new "Same shift, other years" section: any past
  shift (regardless of calendar date) whose start and end time both
  land within 30 minutes of today's, grouped exact vs near-miss —
  doubles as a way to spot a mistyped time (an exact echo across
  several years next to one 15 minutes off is worth a look).

entries.summary: Fix AI Bonus Fact getting cut off to a few words
entries.details:
Several current Gemini models spend "thinking" tokens out of the same
maxOutputTokens budget before writing anything visible. The fact route's
budget of 150 was sized for the reply alone, so on a model that thinks
first, the whole allowance got burned on reasoning and the response was
cut off after a few words ("You've spent", "Did you know", nothing else).
Raised to 800 — the prompt's own "under 220 characters" instruction is
still what keeps the actual fact short, this just stops truncation eating
it before it's written. Bumped the per-attempt timeout from 10s to 15s
to match.

entries.summary: Fix intermittent Dashboard/Shifts slowness, AI-fact loading feedback, two review-found bugs
entries.details:
Performance — root cause of "sometimes slow" on Dashboard and Shifts:
- The Dashboard hero card awaited a live Open-Meteo call with no timeout,
  sitting directly on the render path — a slow/flaky response there
  stalled the whole dashboard, not just the weather badges. Weather is
  now fetched in the background after the hero paints, filled in if/when
  it resolves, and the underlying fetch is bounded to 6s.
- Shifts awaited a gov.uk bank-holidays call with no timeout as part of
  the same Promise.all as the actual shift data — also bounded to 6s now,
  so a cold cache can't hang the table indefinitely.

AI fact button: the loading state now says something after 6s/16s (the
server may be retrying a busy model) instead of sitting on an unchanging
"Thinking of something…" that reads as stuck.

Two bugs found and fixed during a self-review pass:
- On This Day's "past leave" query bound the same date to three
  placeholders, making two of its WHERE clauses mutually exclusive —
  it never returned a single row, ever. Simplified to the one clause
  that's actually needed (the JS-side MM-DD filter already does the
  real "same calendar day, any year" matching).
- Team Calendar's shift-search cache was only invalidated on 3 of the
  10 mutation paths that can change shift data (bulk delete, delete
  month/all/colleague variants) — a stale search result's Edit button
  could point at an already-deleted shift. Now invalidated everywhere.

entries.summary: Give the AI fact button the same retry/fallback-model resilience as screenshot import
entries.details:
It was a single, no-retry Gemini call by design (documented as deliberately
minimal when it shipped in v3.4.12) — fine in theory, but in practice the
